prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 topological insulator, and the first experimental realization of the quantum spin Hall state in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: After the full exchange I keep Kane, Mele and Molenkamp for the two-dimensional quantum spin Hall effect. This is a discovery in the sense the prize criteria use the word: a specific theoretical proposal, the Z2 classification of a time-reversal-invariant insulator with protected edge states, followed by a specific experiment, the observation of edge-channel conduction in HgTe wells. It has been confirmed for almost two decades by transport and scanning-probe measurements in several laboratories, and the interpretation is not in doubt. Round 1 showed that the three-name set is the least disputed on the shortlist: Danielsson moved to the same trio, Mehlig, Eriksson, Johansson and Pearce all list B013 as an alternative, and nobody has proposed a different trio except Lindroth. I treat that as reassurance on the names, not as a reason for the choice. The reason is that the science is mature, the chain from idea to measurement is complete, and the citation can be drawn tightly enough to be accurate.
statement.case_against: The credit is compound, and I will not pretend a three-person cap resolves that. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang predicted the HgTe realization that made the experiment possible and cannot be named; Hasan's three-dimensional photoemission work is a separate decisive experimental discovery that this citation deliberately leaves out; and HgTe edge conductance is imperfectly quantized in practice. The 2016 prize on topological phases is adjacent, though I still judge the overlap limited because that prize concerned bulk topological invariants in quantum Hall and magnetic systems, not symmetry-protected insulators. Applications are still distant. Finally, I am working from recollection of the history and the supplied ballots, not from verified primary sources, and Mehlig and Kroll are right that this attribution is harder to defend than the clock case.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B025 first and says the B013 cut through Kane and Mele, Molenkamp, Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang and Hasan is more arbitrary than the one in B025, where one prediction and one experiment map onto three names.
responses.response: That is the strongest argument against my position and I take it seriously. I would answer in two parts. First, the arbitrariness comes from asking one citation to cover both the 2D and 3D discoveries. If the citation is confined to the two-dimensional quantum spin Hall effect, then Kane and Mele (the Z2 proposal), and Molenkamp (the experiment) map onto the achievement as cleanly as MacDonald, Bistritzer and Jarillo-Herrero map onto theirs, and Hasan and the 3D work are a separate discovery, not a displaced co-discoverer. Second, B025 has its own forced exclusion: Andrei or Bistritzer, as Lindroth and Johansson both stress. So I do not think attribution decides between the two. What does decide it for me is that B013 carries no dependence on an open interpretive question, and Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang is a genuine loss that I would put in the record rather than conceal.

responses.point: Eriksson, Johansson, Mehlig and the chair argue that the credited discovery in B025 is the existence of correlated insulating and superconducting phases at the magic angle, which is secure, and that the open pairing mechanism concerns timing only.
responses.response: I accept the distinction, and it changes my view of B025 a little: I no longer think the open mechanism undermines the credited phenomenon, and the replication across moire platforms is real. Where I still differ is on how much weight an eight-year-old field should carry against one with two decades of confirmation, when the committee is asked to be careful about discoveries whose standing is stable. Twist-angle disorder still makes sample-to-sample comparison uneven, and the prize would be made while the Andrei question is still open. That is why B025 remains my first alternative and not my first choice. If the committee judges that eight years of reproduction is sufficient, I could support the Bistritzer trio, and I would then want the citation to say flat bands and first correlated states explicitly, as the chair proposes.

responses.point: Lindroth proposes Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan for B013, dropping Mele so the experimental side has two names, and also raises concerns about optical lattice clocks and the redefinition of the second.
responses.response: I have thought about the Hasan option and I still cannot support it. Dropping Mele takes out one of the two authors of the foundational Z2 and quantum spin Hall paper, so the prize would rest on one theorist and two experimentalists working on partly different discoveries, a 2D chain and a 3D chain. If the committee wished to honour Hasan's work it should do so as its own prize part later. On clocks, your point that the prize should not hinge on an undecided redefinition of the second is fair, and I add that the lattice-clock concept would stand without it. My earlier reservation about novelty relative to 2005 and 2012 remains, though your and Kroll's argument that the magic-wavelength idea is distinct from combs and ion clocks has moved me to name B006 as an alternative.

responses.point: Kroll asks whether the committee can defend a three-name topological set given Hasan, Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang and the overlap with the 2016 prize, and asks that any citation be specific about the quantum spin Hall edge states.
responses.response: I agree with the last request and I have written it into the citation: the quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 topological insulator, with the HgTe realization, and no claim on the three-dimensional work or the quantum anomalous Hall effect. On defensibility, I think the three names are defensible for that narrower achievement, while BHZ is an unavoidable omission that the committee should state openly. On the 2016 overlap, that prize covered topological phase transitions and the integer quantum Hall invariant, and the time-reversal-symmetric Z2 class is a different object, so I regard novelty as secured. I concede that the clock case has the cleaner two-name attribution, and for me that counts in its favour but does not outweigh the broader scientific consequence of topological classification.

responses.point: The chair asks in the summary what maturity standard should apply between B025 and B013, and whether wider confirmation for topological insulators outweighs its compound attribution and the 2016 overlap.
responses.response: My answer is that the standard should be the same for both: independent confirmation of the credited phenomenon by several laboratories, and a citation that claims only what the named people did. B013 meets both with nearly two decades of evidence. B025 meets the first and, I agree, the second if the citation is anchored on flat bands and the first correlated states. I would not apply a rule that treats recent recognition of nearby fields as a penalty for B013 alone: if the 2016 prize counts against topological insulators then the 2005 and 2012 prizes count against clocks and the 2025 prize against B009, and I do not think any of those overlaps is large enough to decide. So the difference between B013 and B025 is a judgment about how much weight timing and mechanism should carry, not a difference in scientific merit.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept a citation confined to the two-dimensional quantum spin Hall effect, and whether Hasan's three-dimensional work should later be recognised as a separate prize part.
The omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, whose HgTe prediction motivated the Molenkamp experiment, is a real loss that no available three-name set avoids.
How much weight the 2016 prize on topological phases should carry on novelty; I judge it small but others differ.
Whether eight years of replication and the open pairing mechanism make B025 premature or only a matter of how the citation is worded.
My recollection of the attribution history has not been checked against primary sources.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for B013: I have no documented tie to Kane, Mele or Molenkamp, and my work in electron microscopy of oxide interfaces is not close to topological insulators. I disclose again that Göran Johansson is a Chalmers colleague; he does not prefer B013 and that has not affected my reading of his arguments. I would apply recusal-style care only if a Chalmers-related candidate or a microscopy-instrument candidate that touches my own group's work came to the final stage, and none of the current preferred configurations does.
